item.text: {"question_id":"3B.10","answer":"The supplied evidence does not establish that people were durably safer from state and non-state violence by the end of 2023. UNJHRO recorded a 12% decline in documented violations from 2022, and April ceasefires temporarily reduced M23 hostilities, but these are mixed outcome signals affected by reporting limits and did not produce a demonstrated durable, exposure-adjusted improvement (BATCH-0025-E009; BATCH-0027-E006). By late 2023, eastern fighting had displaced about 6.8–6.9 million people; M23 had expanded territorial control, ADF remained highly lethal, and renewed fighting increased political violence involving M23 (BATCH-0010-E003; BATCH-0013-E014; BATCH-0027-E006). The state-of-siege policy, continued under Tshisekedi's government, was reported to have failed its civilian-protection aims while coinciding with increased attacks, state abuses, arbitrary detention, restrictions on dissent, and weak accountability (BATCH-0012-R03-E004). The 30 August Goma operation provides direct 2023 evidence of severe state-force violence against protesters—at least 56 deaths on the official count, more than 80 injuries, and more than 150 arbitrary arrests—with evidence of advance planning and only flawed, limited military-court accountability; the presidential source does not establish a direct order by Tshisekedi (BATCH-0011-E018). Human Rights Watch also described recurring repression of journalists, activists, critics, and peaceful demonstrations, alongside government support for abusive armed groups, while not attributing every act personally to the president (BATCH-0028-E015). Justice legislation, magistrate recruitment, access-to-justice figures, selected convictions, and the ICC cooperation agreement show institutional activity and stated commitments, but not nationwide durable safety, completed remedies, or isolated presidential causation (BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0019-E001). Overall, the end-state is adverse and the severity is at least widespread recurring insecurity with serious state-attributed abuses, but Tshisekedi's precise causal share is limited by inherited conflict, armed-group and foreign involvement, population exposure, decentralized command, and constrained reporting.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0025-E009","BATCH-0027-E006","BATCH-0009-E004"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0010-E003","BATCH-0013-E014","BATCH-0012-R03-E004","BATCH-0011-E018","BATCH-0028-E015","BATCH-0019-E001","BATCH-0021-E007"],"limitations_and_gaps":["No complete exposure-adjusted inherited baseline or counterfactual for 2019–2023 is supplied.","Documented violations and reported conflict outcomes may be distorted by access, censorship, conflict geography, and humanitarian reporting capacity; silence cannot establish safety.","Presidential authority over armed groups, foreign forces, and decentralized provincial commands is incomplete, while national policy continuation and state-force conduct provide stronger attribution than total conflict outcomes.","The supplied justice and ICC evidence records institutional outputs and commitments, not durable nationwide safety or completed remedies."],"corrections_made":["Removed the draft's treatment of ICC cooperation and justice-capacity expansion as favorable end-state safety indicators; retained them only as qualified institutional activity and stated commitment.","Specified that the 12% decline and ceasefires are mixed, temporary or reporting-sensitive signals rather than proof of durable safety.","Preserved the distinction between adverse national outcomes, state-force responsibility, decentralized command, external shocks, and personal presidential causation."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["A complete inherited-to-2023 exposure-adjusted comparison could materially refine the end-state judgment.","Additional evidence on nationwide remedy, command responsibility, state support for aligned armed groups, reporting freedom, and civilian-protection outcomes could change the attribution or severity characterization."]}
